desc:
Rearrange the integer array nums so that values that occur less often come first. Values with the same number of occurrences must appear with the larger value first. All copies of a value stay together in the result.

Return the rearranged array.

For example, [1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3] becomes [3, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2], and [2, 3, 1, 3, 2] becomes [1, 3, 3, 2, 2] (3 and 2 both occur twice, so 3 goes first).
hints: First find how many times each value occurs. A hash map or a fixed-size count array both work.
The sort key of a value is the pair (count, -value). Every copy of a value shares the same key.

A count never exceeds n, so instead of a comparison sort you can place values into buckets indexed by their count, sort each (small) bucket by descending value and read the buckets from count 1 upward, writing each value as many times as its count.
editorial: Count occurrences, then group the distinct values by their count: buckets[c] holds every value that occurs exactly c times. Walk c from 1 to n; for each bucket, sort its values in descending order and append each value c times to the answer.

The only comparison sorting left is inside buckets, whose total size is the number of distinct values. Sorting the whole array with the key (count[x], -x) is the shorter code and is equally fine here at O(n log n).
